title: Galentines Day

jokes.text: It's like Lilith Fair, minus the angst. Plus frittatas.
jokes.setup: Leslie is describing Galentine's Day as a joyful celebration of female friendship.
jokes.punchline: The absurd specificity of 'minus the angst, plus frittatas' as the essential distinctions nails the parody of feminist festival culture while celebrating Leslie's food-centered optimism.
jokes.explanation: This is a genuinely excellent joke. 'Minus the angst, plus frittatas' is perfectly constructed — two parallel beats that work in opposition, and the specific word 'frittatas' (not pancakes, not waffles) is quintessentially Leslie. It's quotable, it's economical, and it could only come from this character. Scores 8+ because it's crisp, original, and does real character work.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Galentine's Day is not a real holiday, but it should be. It's like combining the angst of Lilith Fair with the comfort food of a frittata.

jokes.text: It makes The Notebook look like Saw V.
jokes.setup: Leslie hypes her mother's story as 'the most romantic story ever told.'
jokes.punchline: The comparison to Saw V as the benchmark for un-romantic content is an absurdly specific and funny cultural reference — Saw V in particular (not just 'a horror movie') maximizes the comedic distance.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Saw V' (not just 'Saw') elevates this from a generic pop culture gag to something sharper. The joke hinges on comedic distance — placing The Notebook and Saw V at opposite poles of the romantic spectrum and using the latter as the low bar. Solid structure and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The Notebook is the most romantic movie ever made.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What about that torture porn you watched last week?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's not romantic, Ben. That's just violent and disturbing.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I don't know, the way those people connected over their shared trauma seemed pretty intimate.

jokes.text: 'Are you okay?' 'I am now.' — and the dramatic retelling itself
jokes.setup: Leslie's mom recounts her dramatic ocean rescue romance with theatrical gravitas.
jokes.punchline: The callback line 'I am now' is delivered as peak romance movie cheese — the joke is that this is exactly the kind of corny thing Leslie (and the show) celebrates unironically.
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is gentle — the line itself is a romance cliché played straight, and the humor comes from the audience recognizing the formula. Functional but not particularly original.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie's Mom
dialogue.line: So your father and I were on our honeymoon in Paris, and we decided to take a romantic walk along the Seine at sunset...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. Before you continue, I need to set up a bracket system to rank this story's romantic moments.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, go ahead. And speak clearly — I'm live-tweeting this.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ooh! Ooh! Did you just earn a point? I'm giving that moment a 7 out of 10. Very solid, but needs more passion to move to the final round.

jokes.text: I got to take one of those lifeguard courses. Those guys get all the action. Am I right, Justin?
jokes.setup: Marlene finishes her heartfelt rescue romance story.
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately pivots from the emotional story to calculating how to use lifeguarding as a pickup strategy, then appeals to Justin for male solidarity.
jokes.explanation: Tom's inability to separate romantic advice from personal pickup tactics is perfectly in character. The 'Am I right, Justin?' tag adds a nice layer — Tom is seeking bro-validation from someone who has nothing to do with lifeguarding. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Have you heard the story about when I accidentally ordered 500 pounds of waffles?

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: Yes, Leslie, you've told me this story 47 times.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I know, but I want to tell it again because it's dramatic and you need to hear the drama in my voice.

jokes.text: He's probably married. Or dead. What's the difference? Am I right, Justin?
jokes.setup: The group is debating whether to find Frank, the lifeguard.
jokes.punchline: Tom's nihilistic equivalence of 'married' and 'dead' as outcomes for a man is a darkly funny aside, followed by another 'Am I right, Justin?' — establishing the running gag.
jokes.explanation: The 'married or dead, what's the difference' line has a pleasingly dark edge that fits Tom's cynical-romantic worldview. The repeat of 'Am I right, Justin?' seeds the running gag that pays off later.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Dude, that's so romantic! A lifeguard rescue? That's like the ultimate pickup move.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Gergich
dialogue.line: I once tried to save someone at the beach. Turns out they were just floating on purpose.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: See, this is what I'm talking about. Guys getting action, am I right, Jerry?

jokes.text: But if you find him and he's weird, like a ventriloquist or a puppeteer or anyone who pretends toys are people, then abort the mission.
jokes.setup: Leslie agrees to let them find Frank, but with conditions.
jokes.punchline: Her list of dealbreakers is absurdly specific — not 'criminal' or 'dangerous' but 'ventriloquist or puppeteer.' The clarifying phrase 'anyone who pretends toys are people' escalates the absurdity perfectly.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The specificity of 'ventriloquist or puppeteer' as Leslie's red flags — rather than any rational concern — is perfectly absurd. 'Anyone who pretends toys are people' as the unifying category is brilliant economy. It's completely original, highly quotable, and could only come from Leslie. Justifies 8+ scoring.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Marriage is like death.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: What do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: It's the end of everything you knew before.

jokes.text: I knew, eventually, somehow, being in a relationship with you would totally pay off.
jokes.setup: Ben's girlfriend surprises him with a thoughtful Valentine's Day gift.
jokes.punchline: Rather than a romantic response, Ben frames the relationship in purely transactional cost-benefit terms — as if he'd been waiting for ROI.
jokes.explanation: Funny subversion of a romantic moment — the joke is that Ben's emotional response is couched in the language of investment returns. Solid character work for a socially awkward male character type.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Okay, I will help you find your old flame, but only if you agree to my conditions.

dialogue.speaker: Marlene
dialogue.line: What kind of conditions?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Well, he has to be employed. He has to have all his original teeth. And he cannot be wanted for any crimes in the tri-state area.

dialogue.speaker: Marlene
dialogue.line: Those seem reasonable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Oh, and he has to enjoy the smell of lavender. And he cannot be afraid of heights. And he has to be willing to learn Portuguese. And he cannot have ever been in a blimp. And he has to like his mother, but not too much. And he cannot have webbed feet.

dialogue.speaker: Marlene
dialogue.line: Webbed feet?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I don't make the rules, Marlene.

jokes.text: I bought him some actual towels. He was using a bathrobe. And I bought him some other things that humans usually use, like shampoo.
jokes.setup: Ann explains the Valentine's Day gifts she bought for her boyfriend.
jokes.punchline: The revelation that her boyfriend was using a bathrobe as a towel substitute — and that shampoo counts as a gift — implies he's been living like a feral person, which Ann frames with clinical nurse detachment.
jokes.explanation: The specific detail of a bathrobe-as-towel is a good character reveal. 'Things that humans usually use' is a nice escalating understatement. Works well as efficient character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I got Ann a gift, and I gotta say, I'm treating this relationship like an investment portfolio, and it is finally paying dividends.

jokes.text: Are we talking A.M. or P.M.? Those people are old! Am I right, Justin? / Oh. Justin's not here.
jokes.setup: Tom makes his third 'Am I right, Justin?' appeal but Justin is absent.
jokes.punchline: The running gag of Tom seeking Justin's male solidarity pays off with the deflating realization that Justin isn't present — Tom is left hanging.
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the 'Am I right, Justin?' running gag is well-timed. Tom's self-aware 'Oh. Justin's not here.' lands the deflation perfectly. The gag is set up twice before this and the third beat is the right moment to subvert it. Solid sitcom running gag construction.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: I got him a toothbrush, a bar of soap, and some floss. Things humans usually use.

jokes.text: No offense, but everybody here is terrible at love. Divorced, dating a gay guy, divorced twice, jury's still out on you two. Oh. And, Jerry, who knows?
jokes.setup: Leslie rallies the team before the senior center Valentine's dance, noting they can learn from long-married seniors.
jokes.punchline: Leslie methodically diagnoses each colleague's romantic failures with clinical specificity, with 'jury's still out on you two' for an ambiguous couple, and the final dismissive 'Jerry, who knows?' as a non-acknowledgment of Jerry's happy marriage claim.
jokes.explanation: This is a tight ensemble joke — each beat lands individually (divorced, dating a gay guy, divorced twice are escalating indignities), and the 'jury's still out' ambiguity adds mystery. The dismissal of Jerry's perfectly legitimate claim is a great running joke for the character. The escalating specificity is well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: You know, when you get to be my age, you start to appreciate the simple things in life.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: A good scotch, a solid woodworking project, and the company of—

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Wait, where's Justin?

jokes.text: I've been happily married for 28 years. You've met my wife Gayle many times. / Whatever.
jokes.setup: Jerry offers his marriage as counter-evidence to Leslie's 'everyone here is terrible at love' claim.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's 'Whatever' is the joke — she dismisses Jerry's legitimate happy marriage without engaging with it at all. The audience knows Leslie is wrong but Leslie doesn't care.
jokes.explanation: The joke is the injustice — Jerry has a great marriage and Leslie simply refuses to acknowledge it. 'Whatever' as a complete non-response is perfectly dismissive. The character integration is strong for both Jerry (earnest, ignored) and Leslie (single-minded, oblivious).

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I learned so much from the seniors today about love and relationships. Turns out, I'm doing great. Everyone else is a disaster.

jokes.text: I didn't volunteer. / Yeah, too bad. You got drafted. / Ask not what your old people could do for you. Ask what you could do for your old people.
jokes.setup: Leslie announces Mark and Ann as 'special volunteers' for the senior dance.
jokes.punchline: Leslie misquotes JFK's famous 'ask not' line, replacing 'country' with 'old people,' then doubles down on the misattribution when Mark says 'Terminator.'
jokes.explanation: The JFK parody works because the substitution is both logical (Leslie is making a speech) and absurd (old people for country). The Terminator confusion is a nice secondary beat.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I'm not terrible at love. I've been married to Gayle for over 20 years.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Whatever.

jokes.text: Terminator. / What? No. JFK. / This meeting has been terminated. / That is the Terminator. / Nice. / Where am I going?
jokes.setup: Leslie delivers a JFK parody speech. Mark mistakes it for a Terminator reference.
jokes.punchline: Tom then ACTUALLY quotes the Terminator ('This meeting has been terminated'), Leslie insists it's JFK, and someone appreciates Tom's version — the meta-joke about which pop culture reference is appropriate lands with escalating confusion.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the JFK/Terminator bit works well as a quick ensemble riff. Tom's 'this meeting has been terminated' is the best beat — he's intentionally making the Terminator joke that Mark accidentally implied. The 'Nice.' approval and then someone's bewildered 'Where am I going?' is a good button.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: I don't want to be assigned to the zoning department. I want to work in Parks.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, that's not going to happen. Consider this your deployment.

jokes.text: Come on. This is Armand de Brignac. Jay-Z drinks this. / Yeah, well, Jay-Z doesn't have to perform surgery in an hour. / You don't know Jay-Z's schedule. He's a renaissance man.
jokes.setup: Tom is trying to impress a woman with expensive champagne.
jokes.punchline: When she declines because she has surgery, Tom defends Jay-Z's flexibility as a Renaissance man — as if Jay-Z's schedule is a valid counterargument to her medical obligations.
jokes.explanation: Tom's logic — that Jay-Z being a Renaissance man somehow invalidates her surgery scheduling — is perfectly absurd Tom Haverford reasoning. 'You don't know Jay-Z's schedule' is a great non-sequitur. Strong character integration; this reads as pure Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ask not what your country can do for you, ask what you can do for your country.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's JFK.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, that's Terminator 2.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No, it's definitely JFK.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Come with me if you want to live.

jokes.text: Look, Tommy... / I just want you to know I'm so grateful for everything you did for me. But I only see us as friends. / For now. / But think about how much better our friendship would be if we added doing it.
jokes.setup: Tom has made a romantic gesture with champagne and gifts; Wendy gently lets him down.
jokes.punchline: Tom's response to 'I only see us as friends' is 'For now' followed by the pitch that their friendship would be enhanced 'if we added doing it' — the euphemism and the transactional logic are both perfectly Tom.
jokes.explanation: The 'for now' interjection before a full sentence lands shows good comedic instinct. 'Added doing it' is a funny euphemism that works because Tom thinks he's being sophisticated. Strong character integration for Tom's brand of delusional optimism.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Look, I'm just saying, Jay-Z is a businessman. He's got Roc Nation, he's got sports management, he's got real estate holdings.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown
dialogue.line: Tom, what does that have to do with anything?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm saying, defending Jay-Z might also be a surgeon. You don't know.

jokes.text: Tom's dejected silence / reaction beat after Wendy's rejection
jokes.setup: Tom has laid out his entire romantic case. Wendy says 'I just don't feel that way about you. I'm sorry.'
jokes.punchline: The long pause before the next scene — Tom's silent devastation after a doomed pitch is the joke; the camera holds on his face.
jokes.explanation: Standard mockumentary reaction beat — the silent rejection hold. Functional but not exceptional. The comedy is mostly in what preceded it.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Look, I think we should be more than friends.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Friendship is great, but what if we just added doing it to that?

jokes.text: I just wrote a new song. It's called 'Sex Hair.' It's about how you can tell when someone's just had sex 'cause of how their hair gets matted up in the back. It's awesome.
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to convince the band to play old jazz standards for the senior center dance.
jokes.punchline: Andy pitches 'Sex Hair' as his latest original — the title, the explanation ('matted up in the back'), and the unprompted 'It's awesome' self-endorsement are all pure Andy.
jokes.explanation: This is excellent Andy character comedy. The song concept is absurd but specific, the deadpan anatomical description ('matted up in the back') is very funny, and 'It's awesome' as self-review is perfect Andy obliviousness. High character integration — this joke only works coming from Andy. Earns its 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, I think that went pretty well.

jokes.text: These songs are exactly like the songs you usually play, except instead of modern rock, they're old jazzy standards from the '40s.
jokes.setup: The band resists playing old songs for the senior dance.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's 'reassurance' is a tautology — she's telling them the songs are exactly the same except completely different. The absurd logic delivered with earnest confidence is classic Leslie.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's false equivalence delivered with complete sincerity is a reliable comedic mode for the character. The tautological structure ('exactly the same except entirely different') is well-built.

jokes.text: Dude, Kyle, I'm gonna lose my [mind] on you if you ask me one more time.
jokes.setup: Kyle has apparently been waiting a long time for his shoeshine.
jokes.punchline: Andy — a shoeshine employee — is threatening a paying customer for daring to ask for service, inverting the expected service relationship with complete confidence.
jokes.explanation: The inversion of customer service logic is a reliable Andy gag. Kyle as the perpetual punching bag is an established Parks bit. Functional character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: Can you shine my shoes?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I already shined your shoes!

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: Can you shine them again?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Look, if you ask me one more time, I'm gonna lose my on you!

jokes.text: Ron, I need a half a day off for a secret mission of love. / You're asking my permission to take a nooner?
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Ron for time off to reunite her mom with her lost love.
jokes.punchline: Ron immediately interprets 'secret mission of love' as a sexual rendezvous — the gap between Leslie's romantic idealism and Ron's cynical literalism is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Classic Ron/Leslie dynamic. Ron's immediate reduction of 'secret mission of love' to 'nooner' is very on-brand. The word 'nooner' itself is funny in Ron's deadpan delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, I need to take some time off for a romantic mission.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie, I don't need to hear about your sexual encounters.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, Ron, it's not like that. I'm trying to win back Ben.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I understand. Take all the time you need.

jokes.text: Pick you up tomorrow around noon. / For our nooner, which is a cute word. / Explain it to her later. / Explain what?
jokes.setup: The nooner misunderstanding is being wrapped up.
jokes.punchline: Leslie calling 'nooner' a 'cute word' while having no idea what it actually means, with Ron and Justin exchanging knowing looks, is the button on the running joke. 'Explain what?' is the final beat.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's innocent endorsement of 'nooner' as 'a cute word' is a great button — her obliviousness is the charm. The 'Explain what?' final beat lands well. Good closure on the running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A nooner! That's such a cute word. Like, it's noon, and you're doing something at noon, so you call it a nooner. Why don't we have more words like that? Like, a sevener? A tener?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, a nooner is when two people have sex in the middle of the day.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Well, that's disappointing.

jokes.text: First off, a bear in a paper bag and a heart-shaped balloon... this is a giant teddy bear holding a red heart... a heart-shaped box of chocolates... a dozen red roses in a heart-shaped arrangement... perfume: Yearning, by Dennis Feinstein... finally, the heart of the ocean.
jokes.setup: Ann is being given Valentine's Day gifts.
jokes.punchline: The escalating parade of every possible Valentine's cliché culminating in 'the heart of the ocean' (the Titanic necklace) — the joke is the completist absurdity of getting every single generic gift at once.
jokes.explanation: The joke works through sheer escalation — listing every Valentine's cliché and then topping it with 'the heart of the ocean' is a good absurdist cap. 'Yearning, by Dennis Feinstein' suggests a fake made-up perfume brand which adds an extra absurdist layer.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I appreciate the thoughtfulness, but... did you just give me a card that says 'I love you' made entirely of individual chocolate chips?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes! Do you know how long it took me to glue each chip individually? That's 347 chips. I counted. Twice.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, you could have just... bought a chocolate bar.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But then you wouldn't appreciate each individual chocolate chip! Look, I've catalogued them by size and cocoa content. This is love, Ben.

jokes.text: Yearning, by Dennis Feinstein. / Mm. Ooh. / Dennis, no. No, Dennis.
jokes.setup: Among the Valentine's gifts is a perfume called 'Yearning' by 'Dennis Feinstein.'
jokes.punchline: Ann smells it and immediately recoils with 'Dennis, no. No, Dennis.' — a name-based rejection implying Dennis Feinstein's perfume smells awful despite its romantic-sounding name.
jokes.explanation: The invented perfume name 'Dennis Feinstein' + the personal address 'Dennis, no' is a lovely absurdist bit. Talking to the perfume creator through the scent is unexpected and memorable. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Look, I know they're all clichés. Flowers, chocolates, romantic dinner. I know, I know.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: But you know what? I'm doing them anyway. All of them. Every single cliché in the book.

jokes.text: Do you think they'll get married? / What if they get married? / Would I call him dad then? / No, that'd be too much. / Maybe I'll call him Pappy. Pop. Poppy. Papa. / I'm gonna call him Poo-Paw.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Justin are discussing the possibility of her mom and Frank reconnecting.
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately fantasizes about marriage and spirals through potential grandfather names, landing on 'Poo-Paw' as her final chosen name — the escalation from 'Pappy' through increasingly undignified options is very funny.
jokes.explanation: This is classic Leslie Knope — she takes a hypothetical three steps too far with complete earnestness. The escalating grandfather name brainstorm culminating in 'Poo-Paw' (which becomes a callback later) is genuinely funny and highly Leslie. The rewatch value comes from knowing 'Poo-Paw' pays off. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you guys, Ben's dad is so great. Do you think he'd want to be my stepfather? Because I'm already workshopping grandfather names for when he has grandkids. Like, Grandpa Whiskers, or The Grinch, or Count Chocula...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, what about Gandalf the Gray? Oh! Bumbledore!

jokes.text: What if I told you that you could reunite Romeo and Juliet? Or Brad Pitt and Jennifer Aniston? / Oh, Jen, I really want you to be happy. / Stay away from John Mayer.
jokes.setup: Justin is in a confessional hyping up the romantic mission to reunite Leslie's mom and Frank.
jokes.punchline: Justin breaks from his hypothetical to directly address Jennifer Aniston, giving her personal romantic advice — complete with the specific 'stay away from John Mayer' warning.
jokes.explanation: The sudden shift from hypothetical to direct address to Jennifer Aniston is an unexpected and funny turn. 'Stay away from John Mayer' is the perfect specific warning that lands. The joke reveals Justin's celebrity-obsessed worldview. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is like when Ross and Rachel finally got back together on Friends.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Okay, but that took ten seasons.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We don't have ten seasons. We have like three weeks. Also, we should probably be more like Brad and Angelina.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: They broke up.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, then like Jay-Z and Beyoncé. You know what? Just be like Jay-Z and Beyoncé.

jokes.text: Frank mistakes Leslie for Marlene and tries to embrace her: 'Marlene.' / Oh, no, Poo-Paw. Poo-Paw, no.
jokes.setup: Frank opens his door expecting Marlene; Leslie and Justin are there.
jokes.punchline: Frank, without his glasses, mistakes Leslie for her mother and moves to embrace her — Leslie's panicked 'Oh no, Poo-Paw. Poo-Paw, no.' is both the physical comedy payoff and a callback to the grandfather name she'd picked.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best moments — it works on multiple levels simultaneously. The physical comedy of Frank nearly embracing the wrong woman, Leslie's genuine alarm, AND the callback to 'Poo-Paw' all hit at once. 'Oh no, Poo-Paw. Poo-Paw, no.' as Leslie's instinctive response (using the name she JUST invented) is perfect character comedy. Earns 8+ because of the layered construction.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, I'm not Marlene. I'm Leslie Knope. Although, fun fact, if I ever have a son, I'm naming him Eagleton, after the town I've worked so hard to merge with Pawnee. So in a crisis, you can just call me Eagleton's mom.

jokes.text: My mom always said you wanted to be a lawyer. Did that work out? / No. Never did. Though I did once act as my own lawyer.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Frank if his legal career ambitions panned out.
jokes.punchline: Frank's response — never became a lawyer, but did once represent himself — implies both failure (no legal career) and the proverbial 'fool for a client' joke, delivered without irony.
jokes.explanation: Clean two-beat joke — the 'no, never did' deflation followed by the modest consolation of having once been his own lawyer. The understated delivery implies a dark backstory without spelling it out. Good economy.

dialogue.line: Pathetic alternative credential

jokes.text: You mom was such a firecracker. Smart, funny, sharp as a tack. Such firm breasts. / Oh, that was inappropriate.
jokes.setup: Frank fondly reminisces about Marlene's wonderful qualities.
jokes.punchline: After a string of charming compliments, Frank adds 'such firm breasts' — then immediately self-corrects with 'Oh, that was inappropriate.' The self-aware correction doesn't undo the awkwardness.
jokes.explanation: The joke is perfectly constructed — the compliment list sets up a 'warm old man' expectation, then 'firm breasts' subverts it, then the belated 'Oh, that was inappropriate' adds a layer of self-awareness that makes it funnier rather than less awkward. Good structure.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Leslie's mom is something special. She's smart, she's funny, she's got great legs.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, wow.

jokes.text: I'm gonna throw up real quick, and then we can leave.
jokes.setup: Frank is overwhelmed with nerves about seeing Marlene again.
jokes.punchline: Frank announces his imminent vomiting as a logistical step in the day's schedule, not as an expression of distress — the matter-of-fact phrasing 'real quick' and 'then we can leave' treats nausea as a minor errand.
jokes.explanation: This is a great joke — deadpan understatement at its finest. 'Real quick' and 'then we can leave' transform vomiting from a crisis into a scheduled pit stop. The economy is exceptional (8 words that are individually funny), and it perfectly establishes Frank as a deadpan character. Earns 8+ for economy and originality of framing.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I'm nervous about seeing Marlene. Last time I saw her, I threw up all over her shoes.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: This time, I'm prepared. I brought a bucket.

jokes.text: Valentine's bash at the Bulge tonight. Can get you a drink bracelet. / I can't, I've got to work at this senior center Valentine's Day dance thing. / That sounds amazing. Can we come? / I guess. I don't know why you would want to. / Because old people are funny. / Yeah, it'll be like the Golden Girls.
jokes.setup: April is invited to a cool bar. She explains she's stuck at a senior center dance.
jokes.punchline: Her friends' immediate enthusiasm for the senior dance — 'old people are funny' / 'it'll be like the Golden Girls' — is funny both as Gen-Z cultural logic and as an absurd reversal of expected preferences.
jokes.explanation: Decent reversal gag — cool young people choosing senior dance over a bar. 'It'll be like the Golden Girls' is a funny specific cultural reference for this crowd. Not exceptional but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: We should go to the senior center dance.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Why? So we can watch old people shuffle around and call it a good time?

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: No, it's actually a great community event. Plus the senior center needs support.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: I'm in. Nothing says entertainment like watching people who can barely move try to dance to music from their era.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: That's exactly why I'm not going. I don't need to reduce the elderly to a spectacle for my amusement.

jokes.text: So, Frank, where have you been for the past 40 years? / Oh, you know, here and there. Grenada for a while. Then Panama. Then Afghanistan. / So you were in the military? / Nope.
jokes.setup: Justin asks about Frank's last 40 years; Frank lists a series of conflict zones.
jokes.punchline: The logical inference — military service — is met with a flat 'Nope.' The joke is what WASN'T explained: Frank was in three major conflict zones for unknown civilian reasons, and he doesn't elaborate.
jokes.explanation: This is beautifully constructed. The setup walks us through three conflict zones in escalating order (Grenada → Panama → Afghanistan), which logically implies military service. 'Nope' — with no explanation — is the perfect punchline. The humor is in the absence: Frank was clearly in dangerous places for mysterious civilian reasons, and neither he nor the show explains it. Excellent economy and structure. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I've been in multiple war zones.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wow, Frank, that's incredible. What branch of the military were you in?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Oh, I wasn't in the military.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Then how were you in war zones?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I'm a very aggressive tourist.

jokes.text: You know, I always wonder how different my life would have been if your mother had married me. / It would have been better. / I'll tell you that much.
jokes.setup: Frank muses about an alternate life if Marlene had said yes.
jokes.punchline: Frank flatly asserts his life would have been better — not as a romantic statement, but apparently as an honest assessment of his actual life, punctuated by 'I'll tell you that much.'
jokes.explanation: The joke works because 'It would have been better' can be read as romantic longing or as a grim assessment of his actual life (unemployed, divorced, three conflict zones). 'I'll tell you that much' has a good rhythm as a button.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That was amazing! I really nailed it out there. The crowd loved me. I could feel their energy, you know? I was totally in the zone.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But honestly... I was terrible. I can't sing, I can't dance, and I definitely can't do both at the same time.

jokes.text: Oh, have you got a bag or something? / I have a purse. / Well, give him your purse.
jokes.setup: Frank is panicking in the car and appears about to be sick.
jokes.punchline: Justin's instinct is to give the elderly man Leslie's purse to vomit in — Leslie reluctantly complies. The practicality-over-dignity solution is funny.
jokes.explanation: Decent physical comedy implied by dialogue — the image of Frank potentially vomiting in Leslie's purse is funny but not particularly well-crafted. The joke is mostly in the situation.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: How do you know if a rock performance is going well? You look at the crowd. If people are jumping up and down, throwing their hands in the air, that means it's going great.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But if you see extreme physical reactions... like people are convulsing, their eyes are rolling back in their head... that's when you know... elderly women are flashing.

jokes.text: Uh, I mean, that sucked, didn't it? / Maybe if you sang it like Louis Armstrong?
jokes.setup: Mouse Rat finishes playing 'Let's Call the Whole Thing Off' for the senior dance crowd.
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately breaks character to ask the audience if it sucked — a total violation of performer/audience decorum — and April's suggestion to try Louis Armstrong is both helpful and absurd.
jokes.explanation: Andy's self-aware 'that sucked, didn't it?' is perfect character comedy — he's performing, hates it, and asks the crowd to confirm. Very Andy. April's Louis Armstrong suggestion adds a dry second beat.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: You know, Ann and I have been together for a while now, and I've realized something.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: A good relationship is like finding money in your jacket pocket. You're not sure how it got there, but you're really happy about it.

jokes.text: When you play a rock show, it's easy to know if you're doing great because chicks will flash their boobs at you. But if that happens here, my eyes will fall out of my head and I'll die.
jokes.setup: Andy explains to April how he normally gauges his band's performance quality.
jokes.punchline: Andy's performance metric is women flashing — and he then applies this to an elderly audience with genuinely horrified consequences, landing on 'my eyes will fall out of my head and I'll die.'
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The setup (Andy's boob-flashing performance metric) is funny on its own, but applying that standard to elderly women at a senior center — and Andy's visceral physical horror at the prospect — is inspired. 'My eyes will fall out of my head and I'll die' is a perfectly hyperbolic payoff. High character integration: only Andy would frame performance quality this way. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Our relationship is really working out.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Yeah, you're right. You're a nerd, but it's working.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Did you just call me a nerd?

jokes.text: I might be crazy, but I have this weird suspicion that things are going well with us. / I have that same suspicion.
jokes.setup: Mark and Ann are chatting at the senior dance.
jokes.punchline: Two people in a functioning relationship expressing their own happiness with hesitant over-qualification ('I might be crazy,' 'weird suspicion') is funny as a portrait of emotionally stunted modern daters.
jokes.explanation: The joke is the over-hedging — they're clearly doing well but can't say it directly. Gentle observational comedy, not a big laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: He's not nervous. He's having a complete psychological breakdown. He tried to eat a shoe.

jokes.text: Mark is a great boyfriend. I have no complaints at all. Everything is good.
jokes.setup: Ann is in a confessional talking about her relationship with Mark.
jokes.punchline: The excessively qualified, robotically positive statements ('no complaints at all,' 'everything is good') in a talking head read as obvious tells that she has major complaints — the talking head format makes the subtext readable.
jokes.explanation: Standard mockumentary irony — the talking head says one thing, the audience reads the opposite. The three consecutive affirmations read as protest too much. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Marlene
dialogue.line: Where are we going?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's a surprise!

dialogue.speaker: Marlene
dialogue.line: Oh God. Is this where they take old people to die?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? No!

dialogue.speaker: Marlene
dialogue.line: Because I'm not ready. I haven't written my will. My cats don't even know each other's names.

jokes.text: He's a loon, Justin. / So he freaked out a little bit. / He cried himself to sleep.
jokes.setup: Justin is pushing Leslie to go through with reuniting Frank and Marlene despite Frank's erratic behavior in the car.
jokes.punchline: Justin minimizes Frank's freakout as 'nervous.' Leslie counters with the information that Frank 'cried himself to sleep' — the specificity of this detail as a refutation is very funny.
jokes.explanation: The deadpan delivery of 'he cried himself to sleep' as a factual counter-argument to 'he was nervous' is a great joke. The image of Frank, an adult man, crying himself to sleep in the car during what was supposed to be a romantic road trip is vivid and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Gergich
dialogue.line: Hey everyone, I wanted to tell you about the time I went fishing up at—

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Jerry, you smell like death and I have no interest in your stories.

jokes.text: Mom. / Oh, there you are. / So what's the big surprise? You gonna try to check me into an old folks' home?
jokes.setup: Leslie nervously approaches her mom at the senior center to introduce Frank.
jokes.punchline: Marlene's immediate assumption is that the 'surprise' is being institutionalized — reveals a paranoid self-awareness that she's at senior center age.
jokes.explanation: A decent throwaway gag — Marlene's paranoia about being committed is funny but not particularly clever.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown
dialogue.line: That alimony lawsuit is insane.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, it is insane. But it's my only option.

jokes.text: Come here, sonny. Let me tell you about the Civil War. / Grandpa, leave me alone. You smell like death.
jokes.setup: Background scene at the senior center dance while the main characters observe Frank and Marlene.
jokes.punchline: 'You smell like death' as a response to being buttonholed about the Civil War is unexpected and very dark — the casual brutality of the insult lands because of how matter-of-fact it is.
jokes.explanation: This is a great background gag. 'You smell like death' is a perfect four-word joke — unexpected, dark, and delivered without ceremony. The senior center setting makes it both more and less shocking. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Look, I'm gonna level with you. My strategy is simple: compliment her, make her laugh, then casually mention I own a business.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Women love that. It's foolproof.

jokes.text: You're suing me for alimony? / Yes. / When we were married, I got accustomed to a certain lifestyle, and I'm entitled to money to maintain that lifestyle. / This is insane. / Yeah, it's insane, but it's all I got.
jokes.setup: Tom is pursuing Wendy after his rejection.
jokes.punchline: Tom's strategy to win Wendy back is to sue her for alimony from their fake marriage — and his self-awareness that this is insane ('Yeah, it's insane, but it's all I got') makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: Tom's alimony lawsuit from a fake immigration marriage as a romantic gambit is gloriously insane plotting. 'It's all I got' acknowledges the absurdity while committing to it — this is excellent Tom Haverford character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You know what? You old people are always complaining about your... your back pain and your... your early bird specials and your...

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Actually, you know what? That's not fair. You guys have a lot of wisdom. And you've earned the right to complain about your backs. I respect that.

jokes.text: Three dates. / One date. / Coffee?
jokes.setup: Tom offers to drop the lawsuit if Wendy gives him a chance — he asks for three dates.
jokes.punchline: The rapid negotiation downward (three → one → coffee) mirrors a business deal or hostage negotiation, reducing romance to a haggling transaction.
jokes.explanation: This three-beat negotiation is excellent. The economy is near-perfect — six words, three beats, zero waste. The structure of rapid descending concessions turns romance into a market transaction and reveals Tom's desperation. 'Coffee?' as the bottom of the ask is perfectly pathetic. Earns 8+ for economy and structure.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: What? I'm not being defensive. Why would you even say that?

jokes.text: Hey, you guys sound good. / You really think so? I— it's impossible to tell. It's like bizarro land out there. / As soon as we finish a song, it's dead silence.
jokes.setup: April compliments Mouse Rat's performance.
jokes.punchline: Andy describes the senior audience's silence as 'bizarro land' — his rock-show expectations make elderly polite silence feel like a strange parallel universe.
jokes.explanation: A secondary beat on the rock-show vs. senior-dance theme. 'Bizarro land' is an okay characterization. Not a major joke.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I started as a temp at the Parks Department 40 years ago. Worked my way up through the ranks, became a supervisor, got promoted to manager. Then they outsourced my position. Now I'm unemployed.

jokes.text: Well, what do you expect, you know? They're like a million years old.
jokes.setup: Andy laments the dead silence after Mouse Rat's songs.
jokes.punchline: April's casual hyperbole — 'a million years old' — as an explanation for why they don't react is April's trademark deadpan dismissiveness at its finest.
jokes.explanation: Short and functional. 'A million years old' as April's casual hyperbole is in character. Gets a chuckle.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: So what do you say, Marlene? Want to pick up where we left off?

dialogue.speaker: Marlene
dialogue.line: Frank, that was thirty years ago. I'm not the same person I was back then.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Come on, we had something special.

dialogue.speaker: Marlene
dialogue.line: Frank, you gave me chlamydia.

jokes.text: Yeah, well, these old bags paid for some entertainment, so get... / No, you're right. / Up there.
jokes.setup: April is cracking the whip to get the band back on stage.
jokes.punchline: April calls the elderly patrons 'old bags,' then mid-sentence realizes she shouldn't say that and backtracks — the self-correction mid-thought is funny, and Andy's immediate agreement ('No, you're right. Up there.') ignores the insult entirely.
jokes.explanation: April's self-correction mid-insult is a nice micro-beat. April's standard dismissive persona briefly collides with situational awareness.

jokes.text: Next one's going out to a special little lady named April Ludgate.
jokes.setup: April suggests Mouse Rat play 'The Way You Look Tonight.'
jokes.punchline: Andy, clearly smitten with April, dedicates the next song to her — establishing the romantic tension between them that is about to play out.
jokes.explanation: The dedication to April sets up the comedic-romantic beat that follows. 'Special little lady' in a senior center context is also funny. Gets rewatch value because it's a significant Andy/April moment.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We could go get ice cream.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Ice cream? That's just preparing for death by making yourself diabetic.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Or we could just... enjoy ice cream?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Same thing.

jokes.text: Are you guys-- / Never mind. / Why do you care? / I don't.
jokes.setup: April's friend notices April reacting to Andy's dedication and asks about it.
jokes.punchline: April immediately shuts down the inquiry ('Never mind'), then denies caring when pressed. The self-conscious abort of the question is an April Ludgate signature move.
jokes.explanation: This is excellent character comedy for April. 'Are you guys--' self-censored, 'Why do you care?' / 'I don't.' is four beats in eight words. The denialism is completely April, and given that Andy dedicated a song to her, the audience reads the obvious subtext. High character integration for April's emotional armor. Strong rewatch bonus because it foreshadows Andy/April.

jokes.text: Got a job at a grocery store right out of college. Just for a way to make money. Here I am, 40 years later, completely unemployed.
jokes.setup: Marlene asks Frank what he's been doing for the past 40 years.
jokes.punchline: Frank's life story of temporary grocery employment that somehow never ended, followed by current unemployment — the gulf between 'just for a way to make money' and '40 years later, completely unemployed' told without any apparent distress.
jokes.explanation: This is a genuinely well-crafted joke. The gap between 'temporary job for money' and '40 years later, completely unemployed' is a perfect life-arc joke told in two sentences. The 'completely unemployed' (not 'retired,' not 'between jobs') delivered as a neutral fact is dark and funny. Pairs with the conflict zone detail to paint Frank as a wonderful life-wreck. Earns its 8 score.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We're breaking up.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What? No! April, we can work this out.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: There's nothing to work out. It's over.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, what if we negotiate? I get Tuesday and Thursday make-out nights.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You get nothing. I'm keeping all make-out rights.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's not fair! What about weekends? Surely I get weekends!

jokes.text: What do you say we pick up where we left off? / You're not serious, right? / Serious as a heart attack. Of which I've had four.
jokes.setup: Frank, apparently recovered, makes his romantic pitch to Marlene.
jokes.punchline: 'Serious as a heart attack' is already a cliché — but Frank immediately undermines it by disclosing he's had four heart attacks, making the expression literal and darkly funny.
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the episode. The structure is near-perfect: 'serious as a heart attack' is a common idiom, but Frank's immediate disclosure that he's had four heart attacks makes the cliché literal and devastating. The joke works on multiple levels — it's dark (he's had four heart attacks), it's absurdly specific ('of which I've had four'), it characterizes Frank as someone whose life is a series of disasters delivered without self-pity, and it's perfectly economical. This is what a 9 looks like in a sitcom context.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Mark is like a city built on a swamp. Sure, it's got some nice architecture, some interesting historical landmarks, but nobody really wants to live there. They just visit, take some photos, and leave. The infrastructure is questionable at best. The whole thing could collapse at any moment. And frankly, the tourism board is doing a terrible job.

jokes.text: Blew it. / Take one last look, Marlene, because you'll never see this body again.
jokes.setup: Frank reappears after apparently being rejected by or having a failed conversation with Marlene.
jokes.punchline: Frank's exit declaration — 'take one last look at this body' — is a bizarre combination of wounded pride and delusion about his physical appeal, delivered to someone he's just failed to win back.
jokes.explanation: Frank's exit speech is gloriously absurd. 'Take one last look... because you'll never see this body again' implies his body is a prize being withheld — coming from a 63-year-old man who just vomited in a purse and cried himself to sleep in a car, this is spectacular delusion. High quotability — this is the kind of line people repeat. Strong character moment.

jokes.text: God, why does everything we do have to be cloaked in like 15 layers of irony? / Here's something unironic. Ever since you've been hanging out with that meathead, you've become completely lame.
jokes.setup: April complains to her friend about their hipster-ironic social scene.
jokes.punchline: The friend's 'here's something unironic' followed by a straightforward insult is the joke — the sincere critique is itself the punchline, and calling Andy a 'meathead' is both funny and revealing.
jokes.explanation: 'Here's something unironic' as a setup for a sincere insult is a clever rhetorical inversion. The Andy/April subplot development makes it earn its laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Elderly Woman
dialogue.line: You have a beautiful voice, young man. You remind me of Pavarotti.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh wow, thanks! Is he in a band or something?

jokes.text: Ever since you've been hanging out with that meathead, you've become completely lame.
jokes.setup: April is in an argument with her friend about attitude/sincerity.
jokes.punchline: April's insult — 'meathead' — and assessment that her friend has become 'completely lame' is the kind of caustic dismissal only April delivers.
jokes.explanation: A competent April insult but not particularly memorable. 'Meathead' is a dated insult and the joke doesn't add much beyond establishing the conflict. Below average for April's usual wit.

dialogue.speaker: Elderly Woman
dialogue.line: You have such a nice voice.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Thank you! You know, that's what they said at my rock show. Well, not exactly. They said 'turn it down' and 'leave,' but those are basically compliments.

jokes.text: You know what, we're breaking up. / Fine. / Then you can't make out with me when you're drunk anymore. / Fine. Then I'll make out with Ben. / Pass. / No, he's my boyfriend. You can either make out with both of us or none of us. / Fine. None of you. / Fine.
jokes.setup: April and her hipster friend are having a breakup argument.
jokes.punchline: The breakup negotiation rapidly incorporates drunk make-out privileges as a relationship asset, then escalates to a throuple proposal ('make out with both of us or none of us'), with Ben's 'Pass' on April being the best single beat.
jokes.explanation: This is an excellent escalation sequence. The friendship breakup rapidly incorporating drunk make-out privileges as negotiating terms, Ben's unexpected 'Pass' when April is proposed as a make-out partner (rejecting the implied compliment), and the 'both of us or none of us' ultimatum leading to 'Fine. None of you.' / 'Fine.' are all great beats. The rapid-fire structure and escalating absurdity make this one of the episode's best comedic sequences. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: He's a tourist. He vacations in people's lives, takes pictures, puts 'em in a scrapbook, and moves on. All he's interested in are stories.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Ron why she doesn't like Justin even though he seems good on paper.
jokes.punchline: Ron's tourist metaphor is sharply observed — the extended metaphor (vacations, pictures, scrapbook) builds to a precise character diagnosis that lands as truth rather than comedy, but the metaphor's economy and accuracy give it comedic satisfaction.
jokes.explanation: This is Ron Swanson at his best — cutting through social niceties with precise, devastating accuracy. The tourist metaphor is original, well-extended, and lands as both a great character moment for Ron (who usually doesn't volunteer emotional intelligence) and a satisfying diagnosis. 'Takes pictures, puts 'em in a scrapbook' is an unexpected continuation of the metaphor that makes it feel lived-in rather than constructed. Earns 8+ because this is exactly the kind of Ron moment that fans remember.

jokes.text: I told you so. / It's Duke Silver.
jokes.setup: Ron has just delivered wise advice to Leslie. Then elderly women approach asking for an autograph.
jokes.punchline: Ron is revealed to be 'Duke Silver' — his secret jazz musician alter ego — immediately undercutting his serious sage moment with the absurd revelation that he's a celebrity at this senior dance.
jokes.explanation: Duke Silver is one of Parks and Rec's great recurring jokes — Ron Swanson's secret identity as a smooth jazz romantic musician is perfect character comedy because it's so wildly incongruous with his public persona. The reveal here is perfectly timed: Ron has just been deeply wise and serious, and then the Duke Silver fan moment arrives immediately, undercutting his gravitas. 'You're mistaken, ladies. Move along.' is a perfect Ron denial. High character integration — this is pure Parks and Rec gold. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Duke, can I have your autograph? I love your music. / You're mistaken, ladies. Move along.
jokes.setup: Elderly women have recognized Ron as 'Duke Silver.'
jokes.punchline: Ron's flat denial — 'You're mistaken, ladies. Move along.' — while clearly being Duke Silver is the joke. The authority of 'move along' addressed to adoring fans is absurdly pompous.
jokes.explanation: The follow-beat on the Duke Silver reveal. 'Move along' as a command to fan ladies is a perfect Ron Swanson construction — the dismissive authority applied to an incongruous situation. 'You're mistaken' while being obviously Duke Silver is great deadpan. High character integration.

jokes.text: I thought you were just terrific. / Seriously? / You sound like Dean Martin. / If I were 50 years younger... / Ew.
jokes.setup: An elderly woman compliments Mouse Rat's performance.
jokes.punchline: The elderly woman begins what seems like an innocent compliment but trails off with 'if I were 50 years younger...' — an implied sexual come-on — prompting Andy's 'Ew.' The role reversal of Andy being on the receiving end of unwanted romantic attention from an elderly woman is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A nice callback to Andy's earlier horror at the thought of elderly women expressing sexual interest in him. This time it's delivered verbally rather than visually, and 'Ew.' is the perfect simple reaction. The old-lady version of flashing, as the next line notes.

jokes.text: Wait, who's Dean Martin?
jokes.setup: An elderly woman has just told Andy he sounds like Dean Martin.
jokes.punchline: Andy, a musician, has no idea who Dean Martin is — revealing a generational/cultural gap and characterizing Andy as someone whose musical knowledge is entirely self-contained.
jokes.explanation: Four words. Perfect economy. Andy's ignorance of Dean Martin despite having just performed his era's standards for an hour is a great character beat. The timing — after receiving the compliment, after the 'Ew' — makes it land as a button on the scene.

jokes.text: If I'm not mistaken, that was the old lady version of flashing. / Nailed the gig.
jokes.setup: Andy recounts the elderly woman's 'if I were 50 years younger' come-on.
jokes.punchline: 'That was the old lady version of flashing' explicitly connects back to Andy's earlier boob-flashing performance metric — and 'nailed the gig' follows logically from that: if flashing = success, then this counts.
jokes.explanation: This is an excellent callback. Andy established his performance metric (women flashing) at 11:30. The 'old lady version of flashing' perfectly applies that metric to the senior context, and 'nailed the gig' as the logical conclusion is deeply satisfying. The callback reward is high here — viewers who remember the earlier joke get the full payoff. Excellent structure and character integration. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Is it my fault? Did I do something wrong? / No. Seriously, this has nothing to do with you. / Can we still go suit shopping? / Of course. Armani's having a sale right now. Time to get you a pocket square.
jokes.setup: Tom and Justin process the end of Justin's relationship with Leslie.
jokes.punchline: Tom's devastation about the breakup is entirely redirected to concern about their suit-shopping plans — the pivot reveals Tom's priorities and also shows that the friendship between Tom and Justin was always partially about fashion.
jokes.explanation: Tom pivoting from 'is this my fault?' emotional processing to 'can we still go suit shopping?' in a single beat is a great character joke. 'Time to get you a pocket square' as a consolation is perfectly Tom. Good character integration.

tmdb_overview: When Leslie hears her mom's story about an old flame, she and her boyfriend Justin track him down and reunite them on Valentine's Day. Meanwhile, Andy and his band are nervous about playing a gig at the Senior Center.
insight: Uneven ensemble episode coasts on character charm despite below-average joke density.
